summary: Creates an IANA registry for Level of Assurance (LoA) profiles, which describe how strongly a person's identity has been checked. The registry helps people discover these definitions in protocols that use the idea, including SAML 2.0 and OpenID Connect. It is informational, not a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Some ID cards need more proof than others. This memo makes a public list of the different strength levels so everyone can look up what each one means.

questions: loa in saml and openid connect
what is a level of assurance in identity systems
how do you register an loa profile
where can you find loa definitions
subtitle: A searchable list of authentication strength levels used in identity systems

tldr.problem: Identity systems like SAML and OpenID Connect use the concept of Level of Assurance (LoA) to describe how thoroughly a person's identity has been verified, but there was no central registry where these definitions could be discovered.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6711 creates an IANA registry where organizations can register their LoA profiles by submitting a URI, a name, an XML schema definition, and information about where to find more details.
tldr.outcome: The registry enables systems to discover and share identity assurance level definitions across trust frameworks and protocols, even though the registry itself is not a trust framework and reviewers do not vouch for the definitions' quality beyond checking that they are well-formed.

today: RFC 6711 is an Informational RFC published in August 2012. The Level of Assurance (LoA) Profile registry it established continues to operate at IANA and is actively used by SAML federations and OpenID Connect deployments.

sections.title: The Concept of Assurance Level
sections.content:
When a website logs you in, it verifies your identity in some way: maybe with a username and password, maybe with biometric data, maybe with a government ID. Different services need different levels of certainty. A website selling books might accept a password alone, but a bank needs stronger proof. A Level of Assurance (LoA) is a category that describes how thoroughly an identity has been verified.

Protocols like SAML 2.0 and OpenID Connect allow an identity provider to tell a service provider what level of assurance it has achieved for a user, using a URI like http://example.com/loa/level-2. The problem was that there was no standard way for a service provider to discover what that URI means; it had to ask the provider or look it up in a framework-specific list.
sections.plainLanguage: When a service asks another service to log someone in, it needs to know how thoroughly that other service checked. This RFC creates a central list where each assurance level has a name, a definition, and a web page with more information.

sections.title: The Registry and Its Purpose
sections.content:
The IANA Level of Assurance (LoA) Profile registry is a public list maintained by IANA. Each entry in the registry has four required pieces of information: a URI (the protocol-neutral identifier), a Name (for systems that cannot use URIs), a SAML 2.0 Authentication Context Class Definition (an XML schema showing how to use the LoA in SAML), and an Informational URL (a web page where people can read more about the LoA and contact its maintainers).

The registry is not a trust framework and does not vet the actual security or appropriateness of the LoAs it lists. It is purely a discovery mechanism. A service can look up a URI it receives and learn what it is supposed to mean, find contact information for the defining organization, and read how other services interpret it.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it as a phone book for assurance levels. You see a level mentioned in your login, look it up in the registry, and find out what it means and who to ask about it.

sections.title: What Goes Into the Registry
sections.content:
To register an LoA, an organization submits contact information and four pieces of data. The URI is the unique identifier, typically an HTTP or HTTPS URL. The Name is a human-readable label following a naming convention: it must start with a letter, contain only letters, digits, hyphens, periods and underscores, and cannot be a reserved word like loa1, al2, or 3 (to avoid generic names that do not clearly identify the LoA). The Informational URL must be stable and use HTTP or HTTPS, and should give contact information for the organization.

The SAML 2.0 Authentication Context Class Definition is the core: an XML schema that conforms to the SAML 2.0 specification. Multiple registrations can come from a single SAML schema; in that case each URI gets its own registration.
sections.plainLanguage: When you register an assurance level, you provide its web address, a memorable name, instructions in a specific XML format that SAML systems understand, and a link to a website where people can learn more.

sections.title: Registration and Review
sections.content:
The registry operates under the Expert Review policy defined in RFC 5226. IANA maintains the registry and does a basic check that URIs and names are unique and not reserved. Expert reviewers from a pool of specialists check that each submission is well-formed: the XML fulfills SAML requirements, the name clearly identifies the LoA, the URI is unique, and the Informational URL looks stable and permanent.

Reviewers are instructed to allow registrations made in good faith that meet these requirements, but to reject names that are overly generic (like a simple variation of LOA1) or names that do not clearly identify the LoA being registered. The expectation is a low bar for entry: a bona fide LoA definition with proper documentation.
sections.plainLanguage: An expert looks at each submission to make sure the name is clear, the XML is correctly formatted, and the contact information looks good. The expert does not judge whether the assurance level is secure or appropriate, just that it is well-defined.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content:
RFC 6711 is an Informational RFC published in August 2012. It established a registry that continues to operate under IANA's management. The registry is used primarily by SAML deployments and OpenID Connect systems that need to publish or discover LoA definitions. It serves as a bridge across identity federations, since many organizations now register their LoAs in the central registry in addition to defining them in their own frameworks.

The RFC makes clear that registrations in the registry do not imply endorsement or quality beyond what the expert reviewer confirmed during submission. Consumers are advised to examine the LoA definition and contact the maintaining organization if in doubt.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry has been running for over a decade. SAML systems and login services use it to find and publish assurance level definitions. It remains a simple discovery tool, not a trusted authority on security levels.
